The characteristic polynomial of the given matrix is (t−1)(t−2)2. Solving the two eigenvalue equations gives
E1​=span{(3,−1,3)T},E2​=span{(2,1,0)T,(2,0,1)T}.
(1)
For example, multiplying the matrix by these three vectors gives respectively 1, 2 and 2 times the original vector. The eigenvectors form a basis: the matrix with these columns has nonzero determinant −1. Thus an eigenbasis and its diagonal matrix are
B=((3,−1,3)T,(2,1,0)T,(2,0,1)T),[α]B​=diag(1,2,2).​
(2)

b OurBigBook.com
Write Jr​(λ) for a size-r Jordan block. The characteristic polynomial fixes the total dimensions at 2 and −7, while the minimal polynomial fixes the largest Jordan block at each eigenvalue. Consequently, the blocks for 2 have total size four, largest size two, and at least one size-two block. The blocks for −7 both have size one. The complete list, up to similarity, is
diag(J2​(2),J2​(2),−7,−7),diag(J2​(2),2,2,−7,−7),J2​(2)=(20​12​).​
(3)
These Jordan normal forms are inequivalent because their 2-eigenspaces have different dimensions, two and three.

2A (Complex Analysis or Complex Methods)

Words: 155 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 155
2A OurBigBook.com
At the origin, the Taylor series sinz=z+O(z3) and 1−cosz=z2/2+O(z4) give
f1​(z)=z−3(1+O(z)),f2​(z)=2z−4(1+O(z2)).
(4)
Thus f1​ has a pole of order three and f2​ a pole of order four at zero. For the third function, the Laurent series
f3​(z)=∑k=0∞​(2k+1)!(−1)kz1−2k​
(5)
has infinitely many nonzero negative-power terms, so zero is an essential singularity of f3​.
To classify the point at infinity on the Riemann sphere, use the coordinate w=1/z. Then
f3​(1/w)=w−2sinw=w−1−6w​+O(w3),
(6)
so f3​ has a simple pole at infinity.
For the other two functions, an important qualification is necessary. The poles of f1​ at nonzero integer multiples of π, and those of f2​ at nonzero integer multiples of 2π, approach infinity. Equivalently, their images in the w coordinate accumulate at zero. Hence infinity is a non-isolated singularity of f1​ and f2​. Neither function is holomorphic on any punctured neighbourhood of infinity, so the classification of isolated singularities into removable singularities, poles and essential singularities does not apply there.

The Poincare disc model is the open unit disc D={z=x+iy:∣z∣<1} equipped with the Riemannian metric
ds2=(1−x2−y2)24(dx2+dy2)​=(1−∣z∣2)24∣dz∣2​.​
(7)
This normalization gives Gaussian curvature −1. In particular, a Euclidean curve has hyperbolic length ∫2∣dz∣/(1−∣z∣2); the boundary circle is infinitely far away in hyperbolic distance.

A suitable Poincare disc automorphism is the Möbius transformation
f(z)=1−azz−a​.​
(8)
It sends a to zero and has inverse (w+a)/(1+aw). To verify the isometry directly, note that
1−∣f(z)∣2=∣1−az∣2(1−∣a∣2)(1−∣z∣2)​,∣f′(z)∣=∣1−az∣21−∣a∣2​.
(9)
These identities show both that f maps the unit disc onto itself and that 2∣df∣/(1−∣f∣2)=2∣dz∣/(1−∣z∣2), preserving the Riemannian metric.

dD​(0,reiθ)=∫0r​1−t22dt​=log1−r1+r​=2artanhr.​

One can also verify that it minimizes length of a curve: along any piecewise smooth curve from zero to radius r, the Euclidean speed is at least the absolute radial speed. Integrating 2∣dr∣/(1−r2) is at least the absolute change in log((1+r)/(1−r)), with equality on the radial segment. Thus the answer is independent of θ.

For a twice differentiable function, convexity on R2 is equivalent to its Hessian matrix being positive semidefinite everywhere. Here the Hessian matrix is constant:
H=(4α​α2​).
(13)
Its diagonal entries are positive, so positive semidefiniteness is equivalent to detH=8−α2≥0. The required parameter range is
−22​≤α≤22​.​
(14)
The endpoints give convex functions with one flat direction; strict inequalities give a Hessian matrix defining a positive-definite quadratic form and a strictly convex function.

(x2​−23​x1​)2=41​x12​−1.

The left side is nonnegative, so every feasible point has x12​≥4. Equality is feasible precisely when x2​=3x1​/2 and x1​=±2. Thus the global minimum is
minx12​=4,(x1​,x2​)=(2,3) or (−2,−3).​

Put r2=x2+y2. On the specified domain, r>0, and direct differentiation gives the divergence and vorticity
∇⋅u=U′(z),∇×u=0.
(17)
For example, the third component of the curl is A(r2−2x2)/r4+A(r2−2y2)/r4=0; the other two components vanish because U depends only on z and the transverse velocity is independent of z. Hence the flow is both incompressible and irrotational exactly when
U(z)=U0​ is constant,A is arbitrary.​
(18)
The exclusion of the axis matters: these are ordinary derivatives on the domain, with no assertion of regularity on the removed axis.

b

Words: 105 Articles: 1
5C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 105
b OurBigBook.com
In cylindrical coordinates, the transverse velocity is Aeθ​/r, so its contribution to the circulation is Adθ. The vertical contribution is U(z)dz, the differential of an antiderivative of U, and therefore has zero integral around any closed curve. If k is the oriented winding number of the curve's projection about the origin, then
∮u⋅dr=2πAk.​
(19)
In particular, a single positive winding gives 2πA; reversing orientation reverses the sign. The nonzero circulation is compatible with irrotational flow because the domain is not simply connected. For A=0, an enclosing curve cannot bound a surface contained entirely in the domain to which Stokes theorem would apply.

a OurBigBook.com
A sequence of real orthogonal polynomials consists of real polynomials pn​ with degree of a polynomial n and
⟨pm​,pn​⟩=0(m=n),⟨pn​,pn​⟩>0.
(20)
Orthogonality is relative to the specified inner product, rather than to the ordinary coefficients. A monic polynomial has leading coefficient one, so a monic orthogonal polynomial has the form pn​(x)=xn+terms of lower degree. In particular, the monic degree-zero polynomial is p0​=1.

b

Words: 108 Articles: 1
6D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 108
b OurBigBook.com
Since xpn​−pn+1​ has degree of a polynomial at most n, expand it in the basis p0​,…,pn​. Multiplication by x is self-adjoint for this weighted inner product: ⟨xp,q⟩=⟨p,xq⟩. For k≤n−2, the polynomial xpk​ has degree at most n−1, so
⟨xpn​−pn+1​,pk​⟩=⟨pn​,xpk​⟩=0.
(21)
Only the pn​ and pn−1​ coefficients remain. Taking their inner products gives the three-term recurrence
pn+1​=(x−αn​)pn​−βn​pn−1​,αn​=⟨pn​,pn​⟩⟨xpn​,pn​⟩​,βn​=⟨pn−1​,pn−1​⟩⟨pn​,pn​⟩​>0 (n≥1).​
(22)
For the second formula, xpn−1​=pn​+ a polynomial of lower degree, hence ⟨xpn​,pn−1​⟩=⟨pn​,xpn−1​⟩=⟨pn​,pn​⟩. At n=0, take p−1​=0, β0​=0 and the same formula for α0​. Positivity of the weight ensures that all the squared norms in the denominators are nonzero.

7H (Statistics)

Words: 201 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 201
7H OurBigBook.com
Let S=∑i=1n​Xi​. The likelihood ratio of rate two to rate one is 2ne−S, which decreases strictly with S. By the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the most powerful test rejects for small values of the sum:
reject if S<cα​,Pλ=1​(S<cα​)=α.​
(23)
Under the null, S has the gamma distribution with shape n and rate one. Thus cα​ is its α-quantile, equivalently half the α-quantile of the chi-squared distribution with 2n degrees of freedom. The distribution is continuous, so boundary randomization is unnecessary for 0<α<1.
For every fixed alternative λ>1, the likelihood ratio against rate one is λne−(λ−1)S, again strictly decreasing. Therefore the same region is most powerful against every such alternative. Moreover, if G has the shape-n, rate-one gamma distribution, then S at rate λ has the same distribution as G/λ. It follows that Pλ​(S<cα​)=P(G<λcα​) increases with λ, so the maximum rejection probability over λ≤1 is α at one. Any competing size-α test for the composite null is also of level at most α at rate one, and is bounded in power by the Neyman-Pearson lemma for each alternative. The test is uniformly most powerful for the composite hypotheses as well. This is the uniformly most powerful test for an exponential rate based on the sample sum.

8H (Optimization)

Words: 192 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 192
8H OurBigBook.com
Let p be the row player's mixed strategy and q the column player's mixed strategy. The fourth row is strictly dominated by the first. A useful candidate mixes the first two rows so that their first and third column payoffs agree. If the first row has probability t, these payoffs are 7t−2 and 2−7t, giving t=2/7 and common value zero.
To prove that these are optimal mixed strategies, use the two explicit mixed strategies
p=(2/7,5/7,0,0)T,q=(1/2,0,1/2)T,v=0.​
(24)
Their payoff vectors satisfy
pTA=(0,11/7,0),Aq=(0,0,−1/2,−1)T.
(25)
Thus the row player guarantees a payoff at least zero against every column mixed strategy, and the column player guarantees a payoff at most zero against every row mixed strategy. This matching pair proves that the value of the zero-sum game is zero.
These optimal mixed strategies are also unique. Since Aq is strictly negative in rows three and four, any optimal row strategy gives them probability zero. Against columns one and three it must then satisfy both 7t−2≥0 and 2−7t≥0, so t=2/7. Similarly, pTA is strictly positive in column two, forcing an optimal column strategy to avoid that column; its constraints against rows one and two then force equal weights on columns one and three.

For matrices A,B and scalars r,s∈F, the definition of the trace gives
Tr(rA+sB)=∑i​(raii​+sbii​)=rTr(A)+sTr(B).
(26)
Hence the trace is a linear functional on the vector space of n×n matrices.

b OurBigBook.com
The definition of matrix multiplication gives
Tr(AB)=∑i,j​aij​bji​=∑j,i​bji​aij​=Tr(BA).
(27)
The middle equality uses commutativity of scalar multiplication in R or C, together with interchange of finite sums. Thus the trace is unchanged by cyclically moving the two factors.

c

Words: 81 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 81
c OurBigBook.com
To prove that trace is the unique normalized cyclic linear functional, let Eij​ be the matrix units. For i=j, Eii​Eij​=Eij​ whereas Eij​Eii​=0, so the assumed identity for the linear functional gives f(Eij​)=0. Also, Eij​Eji​=Eii​ and Eji​Eij​=Ejj​, giving f(Eii​)=f(Ejj​). Write this common value as c. Since the matrix units form a basis,
f(A)=i,j∑​aij​f(Eij​)=ci∑​aii​=cTr(A).​
(28)
For n=1 the same conclusion follows immediately from the one-dimensional basis E11​. Finally, f(I)=nc; if this equals n, then c=1 over either specified field. The normalization makes f exactly the trace.

Words: 94 Articles: 1
9F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 94
d OurBigBook.com
Every commutator [A,B]=AB−BA has zero trace, by the cyclic identity. Hence its linear span W is contained in kerTr. For the reverse inclusion, the matrix units satisfy
Eij​=[Eii​,Eij​](i=j),Eii​−Ejj​=[Eij​,Eji​].
(29)
The off-diagonal matrix units and the differences Eii​−Enn​ for i<n span all traceless matrices: a traceless diagonal part is ∑i<n​aii​(Eii​−Enn​). Thus every element of the kernel is a linear combination of commutators, proving
W=kerTr.​
(30)
This establishes that traceless matrices are spanned by commutators. For n=1, both vector subspaces are zero. Notice that the argument needs a span of commutators; it does not assume that every such sum has already been written as a single commutator.

We prove prime avoidance by contradiction. Remove any prime ideal contained in another one on the list; this leaves the same union. If the ideal I is contained in none of the remaining prime ideals, choose ai​∈I∖Pi​. For every j=i, incomparability lets us choose bij​∈Pj​∖Pi​. Set
bi​=∏j=i​bij​,c=∑i​ai​bi​.
(31)
For a one-element list, use the empty product b1​=1. By the defining property of a prime ideal, bi​∈/Pi​, and also ai​bi​∈/Pi​. But bj​∈Pi​ for every j=i. Thus all summands except ai​bi​ lie in Pi​, and consequently c∈/Pi​ for every i. On the other hand, c∈I because each ai​∈I. This contradicts the assumed containment in the union. Therefore
I⊆Pi​ for at least one i.​
(32)

10E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 52
b OurBigBook.com
The evaluation map φ:R[x]→C, p↦p(i), is a ring homomorphism and is onto because a+bx maps to any a+bi. By polynomial division, write
p(x)=(x2+1)q(x)+a+bx.
(33)
Then p(i)=0 precisely when a=b=0. Thus kerφ=(x2+1), and the first isomorphism theorem gives
R[x]/(x2+1)≅C.​
(34)
Since the quotient ring is a field, (x2+1) is a maximal ideal.

c

Words: 128 Articles: 1
10E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 128
c OurBigBook.com
Evaluation at a real point defines a surjective ring homomorphism p↦p(a,b) from R[x,y] to R. Its kernel is (x−a,y−b): subtracting the constant p(a,b) expresses the remainder as a multiple of x−a plus a multiple of y−b, by successive polynomial division. The first isomorphism theorem therefore identifies the quotient ring with the field R, proving each Ia,b​ is maximal.
For a maximal ideal not on this list, take
J=(x2+1,y).​
(35)
Evaluation p(x,y)↦p(i,0) is onto C, and its kernel is J: first subtract a multiple of y, then divide the remaining polynomial in x by x2+1. Hence R[x,y]/J≅C, a field. Finally, if J=Ia,b​ for real a,b, the member x2+1∈J would vanish at (a,b), requiring a2+1=0, which is impossible over R.

a OurBigBook.com
A Cauchy sequence in a metric space satisfies: for every ε>0 there is N such that d(xm​,xn​)<ε whenever m,n≥N. Suppose a subsequence xnk​​ converges to x∈X. Choose N so that the Cauchy bound is ε/2, and then choose k with nk​≥N and d(xnk​​,x)<ε/2. For every n≥N, the triangle inequality gives
d(xn​,x)≤d(xn​,xnk​​)+d(xnk​​,x)<ε.
(36)
Thus the whole Cauchy sequence converges to the subsequential limit.

For fixed m, the reverse triangle inequality gives
∣d(xm​,xn​)−d(xm​,xk​)∣≤d(xn​,xk​).
(37)
The right side tends uniformly to zero as n,k→∞ because (xn​) is a Cauchy sequence. Hence (d(xm​,xn​))n​ is a real Cauchy sequence. By completeness of R, it has a finite, nonnegative limit:
dm​=n→∞lim​d(xm​,xn​)≥0.​
(38)
This conclusion uses completeness only of the real line, without assuming that X is complete.

dm​⟶0.​
(39)

d(yℓ​,yn​)⟶dm​.​
(40)
The conclusion depends on the point xm​ itself, even if that point appears at several indices.

d(xm​,xk​)−d(xn​,xk​)≤d(xm​,xn​)≤d(xm​,xk​)+d(xn​,xk​).
(41)
Letting k→∞ gives the desired bounds. Interchanging m,n also gives the sharper symmetric lower bound:
∣dm​−dn​∣≤d(xm​,xn​)≤dm​+dn​.​

First handle possible zero values. If dm​=dn​=0, the previous upper bound forces xm​=xn​. Thus, if infinitely many dm​ vanish, choosing those indices gives a constant subsequence, which satisfies both inequalities.
Otherwise, discard the finitely many zero values and use dm​→0 to choose increasing indices kj​ with
δj​:=dkj​​>0,δj+1​≤δj​/8.
(43)
Set yj​=xkj​​. The preceding bounds give ∣δj​−δℓ​∣≤d(yj​,yℓ​)≤δj​+δℓ​. For m≥2,
d(ym​,ym−1​)d(ym+1​,ym​)​≤(7/8)δm−1​(9/8)δm​​≤569​<31​.
(44)
For m<n, use δn​≤δm​/8 and δn+1​≤δm​/64 to obtain
d(ym​,yn​)d(ym+1​,yn+1​)​≤(7/8)δm​δm​/8+δm​/64​=569​<21​.
(45)
The same holds when n<m by symmetry; when m=n, both distances are zero. This proves both required inequalities. The adjacent-distance inequality is understood for m≥2, since this subsequence starts at index one and has no y0​.

c

Words: 167 Articles: 1
11G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 167
c OurBigBook.com
We argue by contradiction using the previous subsequence construction. If X is not complete, choose a Cauchy sequence with no limit in X. None of its dm​ can be zero: if dm​=0, then d(xm​,xn​)→0, giving a limit in X. The construction therefore produces pairwise distinct yj​ with
d(ym+1​,yn+1​)≤21​d(ym​,yn​).
(46)
Let Y={y1​,y2​,…}. This subset is closed in X. Indeed, if a point x∈/Y lay in its closure, there would be points of Y tending to x. Their indices must be unbounded, because the distance from x to any finite subset of Y is positive. Passing to increasing indices gives a convergent subsequence of the original Cauchy sequence. Part (a) would then make the whole sequence converge to x, a contradiction.
Now define F:Y→Y by F(yj​)=yj+1​. Distinctness makes this well-defined, and the displayed inequality makes it a contraction mapping with constant at most 1/2. It has no fixed point, contradicting the assumed property of closed subsets. Consequently
X is complete.​
(47)
This is the converse direction of contraction property of closed subsets characterizes completeness.

For a bound state, 0<E<U0​: the Hamiltonian operator is nonnegative, and an energy at or above the exterior potential does not give a nonzero normalizable wavefunction. The Time-independent Schrödinger equation and the hard wall at zero therefore give

Continuity of the wavefunction and its derivative at the finite step gives kcot(ka)=−κ. Put z=ka and z0​=a2mU0​​/ℏ. The matching equation becomes

It requires cotz<0, so solutions lie in the intervals ((j+1/2)π,(j+1)π) for j=0,1,…. Squaring, with that sign restriction retained, gives z0​=z/∣sinz∣. On each such interval this function increases strictly from (j+1/2)π to infinity: its derivative is (∣sinz∣−zsgn(sinz)cosz)/sin2z>0, because the second term in the numerator is positive there. Each interval therefore contributes exactly one bound state if and only if z0​>(j+1/2)π. These are the bound-state thresholds for a square well with one hard wall.
Exactly one normalizable bound state exists if and only if
8ma2π2ℏ2​<U0​≤8ma29π2ℏ2​.​
(75)
The printed strict upper inequality misses the threshold case. At the upper endpoint, the prospective second state has E=U0​ and κ=0. Its exterior solution is constant or linear, hence is not square-integrable unless zero; the zero exterior solution and matching would force the entire solution to vanish. Thus there is still exactly one bound state at that endpoint. The strict upper inequality is valid if threshold values are additionally excluded, but that exclusion is not part of the stated assumptions.

Convergence of a numerical method on a fixed interval [0,T] means that, as the step size tends to zero and the starting approximations tend to the exact initial values,
0≤tn​≤Tmax​∣yn​−y(tn​)∣⟶0.​
(97)
For a vector-valued ordinary differential equation, replace the absolute value by a norm. The interval remains fixed as h→0; a small error at only one step is insufficient.
The order of a numerical method is measured by its defect on a smooth exact solution. With the unscaled residual convention for a linear multistep method, order at least p means local residual O(hp+1); equivalently, the residual divided by h is O(hp). Order exactly p means the next coefficient does not vanish in general. For a zero-stable method, under the usual smoothness and Lipschitz continuity assumptions and with starting errors O(hp), this yields global error O(hp) on the fixed interval. Local order by itself does not imply convergence without stability.

Rh​(t)=C0​y(t)+∑k=1p​k!hk​Ck​y(k)(t)+O(hp+1),C0​=∑ℓ​ρℓ​,Ck​=∑ℓ​ℓkρℓ​−k∑ℓ​ℓk−1σℓ​.

For y(t)=tk, it equals hkCk​ (and equals C0​ for the constant), which can be O(hp+1) only if Ck​=0. These functions can be realized as exact solutions of suitable smooth ordinary differential equations, so this is a genuine necessity test. Thus the order conditions are

The Dahlquist equivalence theorem states that a linear multistep method has convergence of a numerical method if and only if it is consistent and zero-stable, under the standard assumptions for the initial value problem and convergent starting values. Consistency of a numerical method means order at least one, or
ρ(1)=0,ρ′(1)=σ(1),ρ(ζ)=∑ℓ=0s​ρℓ​ζℓ,σ(ζ)=∑ℓ=0s​σℓ​ζℓ.

The root condition for a multistep method expresses zero-stability: every root of ρ has modulus at most one, and every root with modulus one is simple. Usual hypotheses include a well-posed ordinary differential equation with f continuous in time and Lipschitz continuous in the solution variable, a valid step equation, and starting approximations converging to the exact values.

A statistic T is a sufficient statistic for θ if the conditional distribution of the data given T does not depend on θ. For a dominated family with density or mass function fθ​(x), the Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem states that this is equivalent to
fθ​(x)=gθ​(T(x))h(x),​
(106)
where h is nonnegative and independent of θ, and gθ​ is nonnegative and depends on the data only through T.
For a discrete sample space, suppose first that the factorization holds. If Pθ​(T=t)>0, summing over the fibre gives Pθ​(T=t)=gθ​(t)∑T(x)=t​h(x), so
Pθ​(X=x∣T=t)=∑T(z)=t​h(z)h(x)​(T(x)=t).
(107)
This conditional distribution is independent of θ, proving that T is a sufficient statistic. Conversely, let qt​(x) be the common conditional mass function guaranteed by the sufficient statistic property, for every fibre attainable under at least one parameter. Set h(x)=qT(x)​(x) and gθ​(t)=Pθ​(T=t). Then Pθ​(X=x)=gθ​(T(x))h(x). Fibres never attained under any parameter can be assigned any conditional distribution, since their multiplying probability is always zero. This proves both directions of the discrete criterion, including possible parameter-dependent supports.

b OurBigBook.com
The Rao-Blackwell theorem says that an unbiased finite-variance estimator δ(X) of a parameter function τ(θ) can be improved using a sufficient statistic T. Define
δ∗(T)=E[δ(X)∣T].
(108)
Because the conditional distribution given T is parameter-independent, this is a statistic computable without knowing θ. The tower property of conditional expectation gives Eθ​δ∗=Eθ​δ=τ(θ), so it remains unbiased. The law of total variance gives
Varθ​(δ)=Varθ​(δ∗)+Eθ​[Varθ​(δ∣T)].
(109)
Hence the improved estimator has no larger variance or mean squared error:
Varθ​(δ∗)≤Varθ​(δ),Eθ​[(δ∗−τ(θ))2]≤Eθ​[(δ−τ(θ))2].​
(110)
Equality holds precisely when δ=δ∗(T) almost surely under the relevant parameter. More generally, even without unbiasedness, conditional Jensen inequality shows that conditioning on a sufficient statistic cannot increase risk for any convex loss in the estimate, provided the expectations exist. The squared-loss result above is the usual variance form of the theorem.

c OurBigBook.com
Write L=mini​Xi​, R=maxi​Xi​ and M=maxi​∣Xi​∣=max{−L,R}. The joint probability density factors as
fθ​(x)=(2θ)−n1{θ≥maxi​∣xi​∣}​=(2θ)−n1{θ≥max(−L,R)}​.
(111)
By the Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem, T=(L,R) is a sufficient statistic. The same factorization shows that the smaller statistic M is also a sufficient statistic. This gives the sufficient statistic for a symmetric uniform sample.
In fact, the likelihood-ratio criterion for minimal sufficiency identifies M as a minimal sufficient statistic: two sample points with the same M have identical likelihoods for all θ; with different M, their likelihoods have different parameter supports, and so are not proportional as functions of θ. Equivalently, the condition that fθ​(x)=cfθ​(y) for every θ and some positive constant c holds exactly when their absolute maxima agree.
To see rigorously that T cannot be recovered from M almost surely, fix any θ>0. The sample has a distribution invariant under simultaneous sign reversal. If T=h(M) almost surely, the same identity would hold for the sign-reversed sample on another probability-one set. Since M is unchanged by sign reversal, it would follow that
(L,R)=(−R,−L)almost surely,
(112)
and hence L=−R almost surely. But this event has probability zero for a finite sample from a continuous uniform distribution: it entails Xi​=−Xj​ for some pair of indices, including the possible case Xi​=0. Therefore T is not a function of the sufficient statistic M. The pair of extrema is not minimally sufficient, for every n≥1, even though it is sufficient.

Solution

Words: 130
a OurBigBook.com
A Markov chain is irreducible if every state can reach every other state in finitely many steps with positive probability. It is a recurrent Markov chain if, starting at any state, it returns to that state with probability one; for an irreducible chain this property is shared by all states.
For the simple symmetric random walk on Z, taking ∣j−i∣ steps all in the appropriate direction reaches j from i with probability 2−∣j−i∣>0. Thus the chain is irreducible. Its return probabilities are
p00(2k)​=(k2k​)2−2k,p00(2k+1)​=0.
(113)
By Stirling formula, p00(2k)​∼1/πk​, so their sum diverges. The standard recurrence criterion ∑n≥0​p00(n)​=∞ therefore proves the walk is recurrent.
The printed hint's constant is erroneous: the actual limit of k​p00(2k)​ is 1/π​. Its positivity is what the recurrence argument requires, but the reciprocal is necessary for the correct numerical value.

b

Words: 119 Articles: 1
20H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 119
b OurBigBook.com
An irreducible Markov chain has positive recurrent states if the expected first return time to a state is finite; this then holds for every state. A recurrent chain with infinite mean return time has null recurrent states.
An irreducible positive recurrent chain admits a stationary distribution. If such a distribution π existed for this walk, its stationarity equations would give
πj​=21​(πj−1​+πj+1​)(j∈Z).
(114)
Thus πj+1​−πj​=πj​−πj−1​, so πj​=A+Bj. Nonnegativity for all positive and negative integers forces B=0. A constant sequence cannot sum to one over Z, so no stationary probability distribution exists. Hence the walk is null recurrent, not positive recurrent: all its states are null recurrent states. The first-return generating function in part (c) also verifies directly that its mean return time is infinite.

Let un​=P0​(Xn​=0) and fn​=P0​(T=n). Decomposing at the first return and using the Markov property gives the renewal equation
u0​=1,un​=∑k=1n​fk​un−k​(n≥1).
(115)
For 0<s<1, define the probability generating functions U(s)=∑n≥0​un​sn and F(s)=∑n≥1​fn​sn=E0​[sT]. Absolute convergence, or nonnegative summation, justifies the convolution identity U=1+FU. The binomial series gives
U(s)=∑k≥0​(k2k​)(4s2​)k=1−s2​1​.
(116)
Solving the renewal identity gives the first-return generating function of the simple symmetric random walk
E0​[sT]=F(s)=1−1−s2​,0<s<1.​
(117)
As consistency checks, F(s)→1 as s↑1, confirming recurrence, while F′(s)=s/1−s2​→∞. By monotone convergence of ∑n​nfn​sn−1, this last limit is E0​T=∞, confirming null recurrent states.
